title: Safety and antiviral activity of inhaled siRNA SNS812 for treatment of mild-to-moderate COVID-19: a phase 2 randomized trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: SARS-CoV-2 remains a global health threat because ongoing viral evolution and immune evasion reduce the effectiveness of existing therapies. SNS812 is an inhaled small interfering RNA targeting a highly conserved region of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase gene, representing a strategy that may enable broader antiviral activity against emerging variants. METHODS: In this phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 3 days of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to receive placebo or inhaled SNS812 (100 mg or 200 mg) once daily for 7 days (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05941793). Safety was the primary endpoint. Secondary endpoints included the time to sustained alleviation (TTSA) and resolution (TTSR) for prespecified composite target symptoms and individual symptoms. Virological outcomes were exploratory. RESULTS: A total of 135 participants were enrolled, with more than 90% infected with immune-evasive SARS-CoV-2 variants. No treatment-related adverse events or serious adverse events were reported. In exploratory analyses, the 200 mg SNS812 group showed a shorter median time to SARS-CoV-2 antigen negativity (2.9 vs 3.6 days; p = 0.007) and a faster viral load reduction rate (- 0.755 vs - 0.652; p = 0.040), demonstrating dose-dependent virological effects. In the modified intention-to-treat population, exploratory symptom analyses showed shorter TTSA and TTSR for prespecified target symptoms with SNS812 200 mg compared with placebo (median TTSR 6.1 vs 8.1 days; adjusted hazard ratio 2.07, 95% CI 1.30-3.29; median TTSA 3.6 vs 6.5 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.14-2.88). CONCLUSION: Inhaled SNS812 was safe and well tolerated and showed dose-dependent antiviral activity, with exploratory signals of symptomatic improvement in adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 infected with immune-evasive variants. These findings support further evaluation in larger, adequately powered trials, including older and higher-risk populations.

The study enrolled 135 participants within 3 days of symptom onset, randomized to placebo or SNS812 at 100 mg or 200 mg for 7 days. analysis_en.research_question_and_background: SARS-CoV-2 continues to pose a global health threat due to immune evasion and reduced effectiveness of existing therapies, creating a need for antiviral strategies effective against emerging variants. The study aimed to evaluate the safety and antiviral activity of inhaled siRNA SNS812, targeting a conserved region of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase gene, in adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This was a phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 3 days of symptom onset, who were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive placebo or inhaled SNS812 at 100 mg or 200 mg once daily for 7 days.
analysis_en.methods: Safety was the primary endpoint, while secondary endpoints included time to sustained alleviation and resolution of prespecified composite target symptoms and individual symptoms. Virological outcomes were exploratory, and the trial was registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05941793.
analysis_en.main_results: A total of 135 participants were enrolled, with over 90% infected with immune-evasive SARS-CoV-2 variants. No treatment-related adverse events or serious adverse events were reported. Exploratory analyses showed that the 200 mg SNS812 group had a shorter median time to SARS-CoV-2 antigen negativity (2.9 vs 3.6 days; p = 0.007) and a faster viral load reduction rate (-0.755 vs -0.652; p = 0.040).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted inhaled SNS812 as safe and well tolerated, with dose-dependent antiviral activity and exploratory signals of symptomatic improvement in adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 infected with immune-evasive variants. They highlighted the novelty of targeting a conserved viral region to address immune-evasive variants.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest potential for inhaled SNS812 as an antiviral therapy, particularly against immune-evasive SARS-CoV-2 variants, warranting further evaluation in larger, adequately powered trials including older and higher-risk populations.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s exploratory virological and symptom endpoints limit definitive conclusions, and the small sample size reduces generalisability. The evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of prespecified primary efficacy outcomes and reliance on exploratory analyses.

title_zh: Safety and antiviral activity of inhaled siRNA SNS812 for treatment of mild-to-moderate COVID-19: a phase 2 randomized trial.
source_body_en: BACKGROUND: SARS-CoV-2 remains a global health threat because ongoing viral evolution and immune evasion reduce the effectiveness of existing therapies. SNS812 is an inhaled small interfering RNA targeting a highly conserved region of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase gene, representing a strategy that may enable broader antiviral activity against emerging variants. METHODS: In this phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 within 3 days of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to receive placebo or inhaled SNS812 (100 mg or 200 mg) once daily for 7 days (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05941793). Safety was the primary endpoint. Secondary endpoints included the time to sustained alleviation (TTSA) and resolution (TTSR) for prespecified composite target symptoms and individual symptoms. Virological outcomes were exploratory. RESULTS: A total of 135 participants were enrolled, with more than 90% infected with immune-evasive SARS-CoV-2 variants. No treatment-related adverse events or serious adverse events were reported. In exploratory analyses, the 200 mg SNS812 group showed a shorter median time to SARS-CoV-2 antigen negativity (2.9 vs 3.6 days; p = 0.007) and a faster viral load reduction rate (- 0.755 vs - 0.652; p = 0.040), demonstrating dose-dependent virological effects. In the modified intention-to-treat population, exploratory symptom analyses showed shorter TTSA and TTSR for prespecified target symptoms with SNS812 200 mg compared with placebo (median TTSR 6.1 vs 8.1 days; adjusted hazard ratio 2.07, 95% CI 1.30-3.29; median TTSA 3.6 vs 6.5 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.14-2.88). CONCLUSION: Inhaled SNS812 was safe and well tolerated and showed dose-dependent antiviral activity, with exploratory signals of symptomatic improvement in adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 infected with immune-evasive variants. These findings support further evaluation in larger, adequately powered trials, including older and higher-risk populations.

title: Implications for future pandemics from a living systematic review and critical evaluation of observational studies of the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccination against the Omicron variant.
abstract: Reliable evidence on COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness during the period of Omicron variant predominance was essential to inform global vaccination strategies. Our living systematic review, commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO), was established to provide an ongoing synthesis and critical appraisal of comparative observational studies evaluating the effectiveness of vaccines against COVID-19/SARS-CoV-2 infection caused by the Omicron variant. Weekly searches covering seven databases up to 31 December 2022 sought evidence for WHO-approved vaccine platforms, including mRNA vaccines (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273), adenoviral vector vaccines (ChAdOx1-S, SII-ChAdOx1 nCoV-19, Ad26.COV2·S, Gam-COVID-Vac) and inactivated virus vaccines (CoronaVac, BBV-152). We used the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool to assess the validity of estimates of vaccine effectiveness. The review included 79 studies of over 53 million individuals, contributing 2032 estimates of vaccine effectiveness against asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection (36; 45.6%), symptomatic COVID-19 (31; 39.2%), severe or critical COVID-19 (53; 67.1%) and all-cause mortality (2; 2.5%). Structured comparisons of vaccine performance across platforms, dosing schedules and populations, focussed on severe or critical COVID-19 disease. Vaccination was observed to be strongly protective against severe or critical disease caused by the Omicron variant, particularly for mRNA vaccines. Most results were judged to be at moderate risk of bias (361, 18%) or at serious risk of bias (1591, 78%) with the principal concern being confounding. We discuss implications for future pandemic preparedness, including the importance of standardized study protocols; robust data linkage between vaccination, testing and outcomes; and validated risk-of-bias frameworks for diverse observational designs.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines against the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2, particularly in preventing severe or critical disease. The central question is how vaccine platforms perform in reducing the risk of severe outcomes during the Omicron variant's predominance.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review was conducted as a living systematic review commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO). Weekly searches were performed across seven databases up to 31 December 2022, targeting WHO-approved vaccine platforms. The Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool was used to assess the validity of vaccine effectiveness estimates.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review found that vaccination was strongly protective against severe or critical disease caused by the Omicron variant, with mRNA vaccines showing the highest effectiveness. The analysis included 79 studies involving over 53 million individuals, providing estimates for asymptomatic infection, symptomatic disease, severe/critical disease, and all-cause mortality.

title_zh: Implications for future pandemics from a living systematic review and critical evaluation of observational studies of the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccination against the Omicron variant.
source_body_en: Reliable evidence on COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness during the period of Omicron variant predominance was essential to inform global vaccination strategies. Our living systematic review, commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO), was established to provide an ongoing synthesis and critical appraisal of comparative observational studies evaluating the effectiveness of vaccines against COVID-19/SARS-CoV-2 infection caused by the Omicron variant. Weekly searches covering seven databases up to 31 December 2022 sought evidence for WHO-approved vaccine platforms, including mRNA vaccines (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273), adenoviral vector vaccines (ChAdOx1-S, SII-ChAdOx1 nCoV-19, Ad26.COV2·S, Gam-COVID-Vac) and inactivated virus vaccines (CoronaVac, BBV-152). We used the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool to assess the validity of estimates of vaccine effectiveness. The review included 79 studies of over 53 million individuals, contributing 2032 estimates of vaccine effectiveness against asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection (36; 45.6%), symptomatic COVID-19 (31; 39.2%), severe or critical COVID-19 (53; 67.1%) and all-cause mortality (2; 2.5%). Structured comparisons of vaccine performance across platforms, dosing schedules and populations, focussed on severe or critical COVID-19 disease. Vaccination was observed to be strongly protective against severe or critical disease caused by the Omicron variant, particularly for mRNA vaccines. Most results were judged to be at moderate risk of bias (361, 18%) or at serious risk of bias (1591, 78%) with the principal concern being confounding. We discuss implications for future pandemic preparedness, including the importance of standardized study protocols; robust data linkage between vaccination, testing and outcomes; and validated risk-of-bias frameworks for diverse observational designs.

title: Convalescent Plasma Restores Viral Clearance After Anti-Spike Monoclonal Antibody Failure in Immunocompromised COVID-19 Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Individual Patient Data.
abstract: Anti-Spike monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) progressively lost efficacy during the COVID-19 pandemic due to the emergence and predominance of resistant SARS-CoV-2 variants. By contrast, high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) collected from vaccinated donors recently recovered from infection provides a polyclonal source of antibodies that remains effective in clearing SARS-CoV-2 in immunosuppressed patients, unable to mount an adequate immune response against the virus. We conducted a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis to examine the effect of CCP in immunocompromised patients persistently positive for SARS-CoV-2 viraemia following mAb therapy, and to evaluate possible biological factors associated with a favourable outcome. Electronic databases were searched for studies published from January 2020 to January 2026. All studies including eligible cases were considered in the systematic review. Unpublished cases were also collected from investigators of the selected studies. The protocol was registered at PROSPERO (CRD420251142891). Forty-seven cases (30 cases from 12 published studies and 17 unpublished cases) were included. In 33 out of 47 patients (70.2%) with a mAb-resistant infection, SARS-CoV-2 clearance occurred following CCP transfusion, with a mean of 2.7 CCP units administered. In logistic regression, total CCP volume transfused was positively associated with SARS-CoV-2 clearance. In conclusion, CCP transfusion was associated with SARS-CoV-2 clearance in persistently positive immunocompromised patients following failure of anti-Spike mAb therapy.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines the efficacy of high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) in restoring viral clearance among immunocompromised patients with persistent SARS-CoV-2 viraemia following failure of anti-Spike monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy, focusing on the central question of whether CCP can overcome resistance to mAbs in this population.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis was conducted, searching electronic databases from January 2020 to January 2026. The protocol was registered at PROSPERO (CRD420251142891). Forty-seven cases (30 from 12 published studies and 17 unpublished cases) were included, with eligibility criteria encompassing immunocompromised patients persistently positive for SARS-CoV-2 after mAb therapy.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that CCP transfusion was associated with SARS-CoV-2 clearance in 70.2% (33/47) of immunocompromised patients with mAb-resistant infections, with a mean of 2.7 CCP units administered. Total CCP volume transfused was positively associated with viral clearance in logistic regression analysis.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not report long-term outcomes, durability of viral clearance, or comparative efficacy against newer antiviral agents. Additionally, the small sample size (47 cases) and reliance on unpublished cases limit generalizability and robustness of conclusions.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review highlights the need for randomized controlled trials to validate CCP efficacy in immunocompromised populations and to determine optimal dosing strategies. Surveillance for emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants resistant to both mAbs and CCP is recommended to guide treatment protocols.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated convalescent plasma (CCP) as a rescue therapy for immunocompromised COVID-19 patients with persistent SARS-CoV-2 viraemia after anti-Spike monoclonal antibody (mAb) failure. Across 47 cases, CCP achieved viral clearance in 70.2% of patients, with higher transfusion volumes correlating with improved outcomes. The review underscores CCP's potential role in overcoming mAb resistance but emphasizes the need for larger, controlled studies to confirm efficacy, optimize dosing, and assess long-term durability. Given the limited sample size and reliance on unpublished data, findings should be interpreted cautiously.

analysis_en.scope_and_question: The review examines the efficacy of high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) in restoring viral clearance among immunocompromised patients with persistent SARS-CoV-2 viraemia following failure of anti-Spike monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy, focusing on the central question of whether CCP can overcome resistance to mAbs in this population.
analysis_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis was conducted, searching electronic databases from January 2020 to January 2026. The protocol was registered at PROSPERO (CRD420251142891). Forty-seven cases (30 from 12 published studies and 17 unpublished cases) were included, with eligibility criteria encompassing immunocompromised patients persistently positive for SARS-CoV-2 after mAb therapy.
analysis_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that CCP transfusion was associated with SARS-CoV-2 clearance in 70.2% (33/47) of immunocompromised patients with mAb-resistant infections, with a mean of 2.7 CCP units administered. Total CCP volume transfused was positively associated with viral clearance in logistic regression analysis.
analysis_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not report long-term outcomes, durability of viral clearance, or comparative efficacy against newer antiviral agents. Additionally, the small sample size (47 cases) and reliance on unpublished cases limit generalizability and robustness of conclusions.
analysis_en.research_and_practice_implications: The review highlights the need for randomized controlled trials to validate CCP efficacy in immunocompromised populations and to determine optimal dosing strategies. Surveillance for emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants resistant to both mAbs and CCP is recommended to guide treatment protocols.

title_zh: Convalescent Plasma Restores Viral Clearance After Anti-Spike Monoclonal Antibody Failure in Immunocompromised COVID-19 Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Individual Patient Data.
source_body_en: Anti-Spike monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) progressively lost efficacy during the COVID-19 pandemic due to the emergence and predominance of resistant SARS-CoV-2 variants. By contrast, high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) collected from vaccinated donors recently recovered from infection provides a polyclonal source of antibodies that remains effective in clearing SARS-CoV-2 in immunosuppressed patients, unable to mount an adequate immune response against the virus. We conducted a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis to examine the effect of CCP in immunocompromised patients persistently positive for SARS-CoV-2 viraemia following mAb therapy, and to evaluate possible biological factors associated with a favourable outcome. Electronic databases were searched for studies published from January 2020 to January 2026. All studies including eligible cases were considered in the systematic review. Unpublished cases were also collected from investigators of the selected studies. The protocol was registered at PROSPERO (CRD420251142891). Forty-seven cases (30 cases from 12 published studies and 17 unpublished cases) were included. In 33 out of 47 patients (70.2%) with a mAb-resistant infection, SARS-CoV-2 clearance occurred following CCP transfusion, with a mean of 2.7 CCP units administered. In logistic regression, total CCP volume transfused was positively associated with SARS-CoV-2 clearance. In conclusion, CCP transfusion was associated with SARS-CoV-2 clearance in persistently positive immunocompromised patients following failure of anti-Spike mAb therapy.

title: Timing, Titre, and Host Determinants of Convalescent Plasma Efficacy in COVID-19: A Systematic Review With Design-Stratified Narrative Synthesis.
abstract: The efficacy of convalescent plasma (CP) in COVID-19 has been contested, with large randomized trials producing conflicting results that led to recommendations against routine use. We performed a systematic review with design-stratified narrative synthesis (PRISMA 2020; SWiM; OSF: https://osf.io/tjcuq) to test whether these conflicting outcomes can be reconciled through three interacting determinants-timing, antibody titre, and host characteristics-using a standardized 91-field extraction matrix applied to each study. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched through May 2026. Thirty-one studies (20,793 patients; 8 RCTs, 23 observational) were included. The synthesis indicates that CP is effective, but only under a specific convergence of conditions: when administered early in the disease course, with sufficient antibody titre, to seronegative or immunocompromised hosts who have not yet mounted an endogenous antibody response. Among RCTs analysing timing, 4 of 6 found benefit with earlier administration; for titre, 3 of 4 RCTs with explicit comparisons found benefit with higher-titre CP; and two large RCTs (combined n = 12,522) demonstrated preferential benefit in seronegative recipients. This interpretation is consistent with modelling estimates that CP, deployed largely to hospitalised patients, nonetheless saved tens of thousands of lives in the United States during the first pandemic year, an effect attributed to the subset treated early enough to modify disease progression. A second, previously unquantified finding concerns antibody class: characterisation of non-IgG immunoglobulins was nearly absent, with only 2 of 31 studies-both from our group-reporting IgA or IgM data, despite evidence that IgA and IgM are among the most potent neutralising classes against SARS-CoV-2. This hypothesis-generating observation identifies a systematic gap in CP product assessment. These findings reframe CP efficacy from a binary question to a conditional one and provide a template for the precision deployment of passive immunotherapy in future pandemics.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review resolves conflicting evidence on convalescent plasma (CP) efficacy in COVID-19 by identifying three critical determinants: early administration, high antibody titre, and host seronegativity or immunocompromise. Among 31 studies (20,793 patients), randomized trials showed benefit when CP was given early (4/6 trials) or with higher titres (3/4 trials), particularly in seronegative recipients (two large RCTs, n=12,522). However, a major evidence gap persists: only 2 studies assessed non-IgG immunoglobulins (IgA/IgM), despite their potential potency. The review reframes CP efficacy as conditional and provides a template for precision deployment in future pandemics, emphasizing the need for standardized IgA/IgM quantification and targeted clinical strategies.

title: Association between COVID-19 by variant period and delivery-related outcomes in the United States.
abstract: BACKGROUND: COVID-19 has been associated with adverse obstetric outcomes, but the magnitude of maternal and fetal risk may have varied across viral variant periods. OBJECTIVE: To assess the association between COVID-19 infection and delivery-related in-hospital and 90-day mortality, severe maternal morbidity (SMM), fetal outcomes (fetal death and preterm birth), and a set of utilization measures (including cesarean delivery, ICU admission, costs, and hospital length of stay [LOS]) in the United States. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using delivery-related hospitalizations discharged between April 1, 2020, and March 31, 2023, from the Premier Healthcare Database. Regression modeling was conducted to evaluate variant-period-specific associations between COVID-19 exposure and key outcomes while controlling for a broad set of maternal risk factors. RESULTS: Of the 2,561,615 evaluated delivery-related discharges, 53,226 (2.08%) were diagnosed with COVID-19. COVID-19 was associated with higher adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality across the Pre-Alpha, Alpha, Delta, and first Omicron phases (aOR [p-adj]: 13.11 [<.001], 13.03 [<.001], 29.47 [<.001], and 3.55 [.04]), respectively. Maternal COVID-19 infection was further associated with increased odds of fetal death at 20 or more weeks of gestation across the Pre-Alpha (aOR: 1.53 [1.28-1.83, < .001]) and Delta (3.37 [2.95-3.84, < .001]) phases. The odds of experiencing any SMM, ICU admission, or preterm birth were significantly higher across all phases of the pandemic, whereas the odds of cesarean delivery were significantly higher during all but the Alpha and first Omicron phases. COVID-19 infection was associated with increased LOS and hospital costs throughout all variant phases. CONCLUSIONS: COVID-19 infection during delivery was associated with higher odds of maternal, fetal, and utilization outcomes at varying stages of the pandemic, with the most notable effect during the Delta period. These findings provide insight into the variant-dependent obstetric burden of COVID-19 and for maternal health surveillance and clinical preparedness during future infectious disease outbreaks.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding the variation in maternal and fetal risks associated with different SARS-CoV-2 variant periods during the pandemic. The background highlights that COVID-19 has been linked to adverse obstetric outcomes, but the extent of these risks may differ across viral variant periods.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using delivery-related hospitalizations from the Premier Healthcare Database, covering discharges between April 1, 2020, and March 31, 2023. The study included 2,561,615 delivery-related discharges, of which 53,226 were diagnosed with COVID-19.
analysis.methods: The study employed regression modeling to evaluate variant-period-specific associations between COVID-19 exposure and key outcomes, adjusting for a broad set of maternal risk factors. The analysis was based on data from the Premier Healthcare Database.
analysis.main_results: Of the 2,561,615 delivery-related discharges, 53,226 (2.08%) were diagnosed with COVID-19. The adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for in-hospital mortality were significantly higher during the Pre-Alpha, Alpha, Delta, and first Omicron phases, with the most pronounced effect observed during the Delta period.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of variant-dependent obstetric risks associated with SARS-CoV-2, emphasizing the increased severity during the Delta period. This study provides novel insights into how different viral variants may influence maternal and fetal outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the understanding of variant-specific obstetric burdens of SARS-CoV-2, supporting targeted maternal health surveillance and clinical preparedness during future infectious disease outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on administrative data, which may introduce biases and missing information. Despite these limitations, the evidence is strong, with statistically significant associations observed across multiple variant periods.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the association between SARS-CoV-2 variant periods and delivery-related outcomes in the United States. It finds that maternal and fetal risks varied across different phases of the pandemic, with the Delta variant showing the most significant impact. The research highlights the importance of variant-specific surveillance and preparedness in obstetric care. While the study uses retrospective data from the Premier Healthcare Database, the results are robust, with adjusted odds ratios indicating higher mortality and morbidity during the Delta period. The findings suggest that future outbreaks may require tailored approaches to maternal and fetal health monitoring based on viral variants.

title: ‘COVID kills, and it's not joking around’: Perceptions and experiences of COVID-19 in Soweto, South Africa
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic intensified existing social and gender inequalities, disproportionately affecting Black women living in communities like Soweto, South Africa. This paper primarily draws on qualitative data from 25 in-depth interviews conducted in 2021, complemented by descriptive survey data from 204 women collected between 2020 and 2021. We employed inductive thematic analysis guided by the socio-ecological model to examine how intersecting individual, interpersonal, community and societal factors shaped women's experiences during the pandemic. Women played vital caregiving roles, supporting families and communities despite considerable personal stress linked to fears of infection, violence, isolation and economic hardship. On an interpersonal level, stigma related to COVID-19 severely disrupted social bonds, causing mistrust and exclusion within communities. At the societal level, pre-existing distrust in government institutions worsened, contributing to vaccine hesitancy. The widespread looting and unrest observed in Soweto during lockdowns are interpreted as collective resistance reflecting the community's perceived right to survival and fair treatment amid structural neglect. We argue that public health responses must adopt multi-level strategies that recognise women's crucial caregiving roles, address stigma through community engagement, rebuild institutional trust and promote economic justice.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines how the COVID-19 pandemic, caused by SARS-CoV-2, disproportionately impacted Black women in Soweto, South Africa, focusing on intersecting social and gender inequalities and their lived experiences during the pandemic.

analysis.summary_en: This review highlights the disproportionate impact of COVID-19 on Black women in Soweto, South Africa, emphasizing how intersecting social and gender inequalities shaped their experiences. Stigma disrupted social cohesion, exacerbating mistrust and exclusion. The review underscores the need for public health strategies that recognize women's roles, address stigma through community engagement, rebuild trust in institutions, and address economic injustices to mitigate the pandemic's long-term effects.

title: Psychological interventions to improve maternal mental health and resilience during pregnancy in the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review.
abstract: BACKGROUND: During the COVID-19 pandemic, pregnant women experienced increased psychological distress, while access to routine mental health care was often disrupted. Psychological interventions may provide an effective strategy to support maternal mental health under these circumstances. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review aimed to provide an overview of psychological interventions for pregnant women during the COVID-19 pandemic and to evaluate their effectiveness in reducing distress and enhancing resilience. METHODS: A systematic search of four databases was conducted up to 3 September 2025. Randomised and non-randomised studies evaluating psychological interventions during pregnancy were included. RESULTS: Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions included cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, psychoeducation, and other psychological approaches delivered through individual, group, digital, or hybrid formats. Most studies reported reductions in depression, anxiety, or stress, and some found improvements in resilience-related factors. However, the methodological quality was modest; with heterogeneous outcome measures and limited follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, psychological interventions adapted for digital or hybrid delivery show promise for improving maternal emotional well-being in times of crises. The findings suggest that accessible and scalable psychological interventions may support maternal mental health during crisis situations when routine care is disrupted. Future research should prioritize larger, methodologically rigorous trials with standardized outcomes, and longer follow-up periods.
journal: Journal of Psychosomatic Obstetrics and Gynaecology

METHODS: A systematic search of four databases was conducted up to 3 September 2025. Randomised and non-randomised studies evaluating psychological interventions during pregnancy were included. RESULTS: Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions included cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, psychoeducation, and other psychological approaches delivered through individual, group, digital, or hybrid formats. Most studies reported reductions in depression, anxiety, or stress, and some found improvements in resilience-related factors. However, the methodological quality was modest; with heterogeneous outcome measures and limited follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, psychological interventions adapted for digital or hybrid delivery show promise for improving maternal emotional well-being in times of crises. The findings suggest that accessible and scalable psychological interventions may support maternal mental health during crisis situations when routine care is disrupted. Future research should prioritize larger, methodologically rigorous trials with standardized outcomes, and longer follow-up periods.

title: Effectiveness of Omicron JN.1 vaccination against infection with JN.1-derived SARS-CoV-2 subvariants in a prospective cohort study in the Netherlands
abstract: INTRODUCTION: We estimated vaccine effectiveness (VE) of JN.1 COVID-19 vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 infection by (sub)variant between 23 September 2024 and 23 February 2025. METHODS: JN.1 vaccine-eligible participants of an ongoing prospective cohort study (VAccine Study COvid-19; VASCO) were included: individuals aged ≥60 years, and individuals aged <60 years with a medical risk condition or who were healthcare workers. In VASCO, questionnaire and serology data are regularly collected and self-tests are provided. SARS-CoV-2 infection was based on reported positive self-tests and/or anti-nucleoprotein serology results. The variant of infection was determined by whole genome sequencing of viral genetic material in positive self-tests. VE against infection was estimated using Cox regression with JN.1-vaccination as time-varying exposure, and VE against JN.1 subvariants KP.3.1.1 and XEC using multinomial logistic regression with matching of infected and uninfected participants by calendar week. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, education level, medical risk condition and SARS-CoV-2 infection history. RESULTS: Of 4490 JN.1-vaccine eligible participants <60 years, 1283 (29%) were vaccinated. Of 19,349 participants ≥60 years, 14,400 (74%) were vaccinated. During follow-up 2142 infections occurred, of which the majority was self-reported (72%). VE was 16% (95%CI: -11-36) in participants <60 years and 13% (95%CI: 2-23) in participants ≥60 years. VE against KP.3.1.1 (n = 251;27%) did not differ significantly from the VE against XEC (n = 195;5%)(OR:1.3; 0.8-2.1). CONCLUSION: We found that, during a 5-month study period with low incidence, JN.1-vaccination provided limited added protection in preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection. The observed VE estimates indicate potentially lower protection against XEC than KP.3.1.1, but the power to detect such a difference was low.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to estimate the effectiveness of JN.1 vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 infection by (sub)variant during a specific period.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective cohort study was conducted in the Netherlands, including JN.1 vaccine-eligible participants aged ≥60 years and those <60 years with medical risk conditions or healthcare worker status. Of 19,349 participants ≥60 years, 14,400 (74%) were vaccinated.
analysis.methods: The study used whole genome sequencing of viral genetic material from positive self-tests to determine the variant of infection. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated using Cox regression for overall infection and multinomial logistic regression for subvariants KP.3.1.1 and XEC, with matching of infected and uninfected participants by calendar week. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, education level, medical risk condition, and SARS-CoV-2 infection history.
analysis.main_results: Of 4490 JN.1-vaccine eligible participants <60 years, 1283 (29%) were vaccinated. During follow-up, 2142 infections occurred, with the majority self-reported. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The observed VE estimates suggest potentially lower protection against XEC than KP.3.1.1, although the power to detect such a difference was low.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the understanding of vaccine effectiveness against emerging subvariants of SARS-CoV-2, particularly in the context of low incidence periods, and highlight the need for further research on subvariant-specific protection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted during a period of low incidence, which may limit the generalisability of the findings. The power to detect differences in VE against subvariants was low, and the results should be interpreted with caution.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effectiveness of JN.1 vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 infection by subvariant in a prospective cohort study in the Netherlands. The research focused on estimating vaccine effectiveness (VE) during a 5-month period with low incidence. Participants included individuals aged ≥60 years and those <60 years with medical risk conditions or healthcare worker status. The study used whole genome sequencing to identify variants and applied Cox and multinomial logistic regression to estimate VE. Results showed limited added protection from JN.1 vaccination, with VE estimates of 16% and 13% in younger and older participants, respectively. The study noted that the power to detect differences in VE against subvariants like XEC and KP.3.1.1 was low. These findings have implications for understanding vaccine efficacy against emerging subvariants and suggest the need for further research. The study's limitations include its low incidence setting and limited statistical power to discern subvariant-specific differences, which affects the strength of the evidence.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估 JN.1 疫苗接种 在特定时期内对抗(亚)变体 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染的有效性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 一项前瞻性 队列研究 研究在荷兰进行,包括符合 JN.1 队列研究 资格的年龄 ≥ 60 岁的参与者以及具有医疗风险状况或医护人员身份的 <60 岁参与者。在 19,349 名 60 岁以上参与者中,有 14,400 人 (74%) 接种了疫苗。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用来自阳性自检的病毒遗传物质的完整 基因组 测序来确定感染的变异。疫苗 的有效性是使用总体感染的 Cox 回归和子变体 KP.3.1.1 和 XEC 的多项逻辑回归进行估计的,并按日历周匹配感染和未感染的参与者。模型根据年龄组、性别、教育水平、医疗风险状况和 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染史进行调整。
elements_zh.main_results: 在 4490 名 60 岁以下符合 JN.1-疫苗 资格的参与者中,1283 名 (29%) 接种了疫苗。在随访期间,发生了 2142 例感染,其中大多数是自我报告的。疫苗 在 60 岁以下的参与者中的有效性为 16% (95%CI: -11-36),在 60 岁以上的参与者中的有效性为 13% (95%CI: 2-23)。VE 针对 KP.3.1.1 (n = 251;27%) 与 VE 针对 XEC (n = 195;5%) 没有显着差异 (OR:1.3;0.8-2.1)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 观察到的 VE 估计表明对 XEC 的保护可能低于 KP.3.1.1,尽管检测这种差异的能力较低。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现有助于理解 疫苗 针对 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 新兴亚变体的有效性,特别是在 发病率 周期较低的情况下,并强调需要进一步研究亚变体特异性保护。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究是在 发病率 较低的时期进行的,这可能会限制研究结果的普遍性。检测 VE 与亚变体差异的能力较低,应谨慎解释结果。

analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The observed VE estimates suggest potentially lower protection against XEC than KP.3.1.1, although the power to detect such a difference was low.

source_body_en: INTRODUCTION: We estimated vaccine effectiveness (VE) of JN.1 COVID-19 vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 infection by (sub)variant between 23 September 2024 and 23 February 2025. METHODS: JN.1 vaccine-eligible participants of an ongoing prospective cohort study (VAccine Study COvid-19; VASCO) were included: individuals aged ≥60 years, and individuals aged <60 years with a medical risk condition or who were healthcare workers. In VASCO, questionnaire and serology data are regularly collected and self-tests are provided. SARS-CoV-2 infection was based on reported positive self-tests and/or anti-nucleoprotein serology results. The variant of infection was determined by whole genome sequencing of viral genetic material in positive self-tests. VE against infection was estimated using Cox regression with JN.1-vaccination as time-varying exposure, and VE against JN.1 subvariants KP.3.1.1 and XEC using multinomial logistic regression with matching of infected and uninfected participants by calendar week. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, education level, medical risk condition and SARS-CoV-2 infection history. RESULTS: Of 4490 JN.1-vaccine eligible participants <60 years, 1283 (29%) were vaccinated. Of 19,349 participants ≥60 years, 14,400 (74%) were vaccinated. During follow-up 2142 infections occurred, of which the majority was self-reported (72%). VE was 16% (95%CI: -11-36) in participants <60 years and 13% (95%CI: 2-23) in participants ≥60 years. VE against KP.3.1.1 (n = 251;27%) did not differ significantly from the VE against XEC (n = 195;5%)(OR:1.3; 0.8-2.1). CONCLUSION: We found that, during a 5-month study period with low incidence, JN.1-vaccination provided limited added protection in preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection. title: Prevalence of hypertension in severe vs. non-severe COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Although numerous studies have investigated the association between hypertension and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) severity, differences in study characteristics have limited the consistency and generalizability of the available evidence. This systematic review and meta-analysis systematically evaluated the association between hypertension and COVID-19 severity by synthesizing evidence from 30 studies involving 15,549 participants comparing the prevalence of hypertension in non-severe and severe COVID-19 patients. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 and τ2 statistics, while subgroup analyses and meta-regression examined the effects of region, sample size, study quality, age, and gender. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. Hypertension was more frequently observed in severe COVID-19 cases across the included studies with a pooled odds ratio (OR) of 2.73 (95% CI: 1.85-4.02, p < 0.00001), However, substantial heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 88%), limiting the precision of the pooled estimate. Subgroup analysis showed that sample size, NOS scores, and age did not significantly explain heterogeneity, with gender composition also not significantly associated with effect size (β = 0.021, p = 0.38). Funnel plot analysis and Egger's test showed no significant publication bias. Overall, hypertension was associated with an increased likelihood of severe COVID-19, although the high level of heterogeneity suggests that the findings should be interpreted with caution. These findings contribute to the understanding of the association between hypertension and COVID-19 severity and may inform clinical risk stratification and public health decision-making.

title: Epidemiology and mortality among hospital-acquired cases of COVID-19 in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods: A data-linkage study in Victoria, Australia.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to compare the epidemiology and mortality of hospital-acquired versus non-hospital-acquired COVID-19 infections among hospitalised patients. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of COVID‐19 hospitalisations in Victoria, Australia (January 2021-June 2024), using linked state surveillance systems. Episodes were classified as hospital acquired if the first positive test occurred ≥8 days post admission. Age, sex, intensive care unit admission and 30‐day mortality were compared between hospital-acquired and non‐hospital-acquired cases across pre‐Omicron and Omicron periods. RESULTS: Of 6,485 hospital-acquired and 62,670 non-hospital-acquired episodes, median age for hospital-acquired versus non-hospital-acquired cases was 77.8 versus 77.6 years before Omicron and 52.6 versus 73.1 years during Omicron. Monthly proportion of hospital-acquired cases increased during Omicron (range: 1% to 21%). Case fatality rates were higher in hospital-acquired than in non-hospital-acquired cases, with a larger difference before the Omicron (incidence rate ratio: 4.49, 95% confidence interval: 2.02, 9.99) than during the Omicron period (incidence rate ratio: 1.62, 95% confidence interval: 1.44, 1.82). Intensive care unit admission was associated with 30-day mortality for hospital-acquired (adjusted odds ratio: 4.4, 95% confidence interval: 2.3-8.4) and non‐hospital-acquired cases (adjusted odds ratio: 4.0, 95% confidence interval: 3.5-4.7). CONCLUSIONS: Hospital-acquired COVID-19 infections remain significant, associated with higher mortality rates than non-hospital-acquired infection and disproportionately affecting older patients. IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH: Our findings underscore the need for robust hospital COVID-19 infection prevention strategies.

Episodes were classified as hospital acquired if the first positive test occurred ≥8 days post admission. Age, sex, intensive care unit admission and 30‐day mortality were compared between hospital-acquired and non‐hospital-acquired cases across pre‐Omicron and Omicron periods. Results Of 6,485 hospital-acquired and 62,670 non-hospital-acquired episodes, median age for hospital-acquired versus non-hospital-acquired cases was 77.8 versus 77.6 years before Omicron and 52.6 versus 73.1 years during Omicron. Monthly proportion of hospital-acquired cases increased during Omicron (range: 1% to 21%). Case fatality rates were higher in hospital-acquired than in non-hospital-acquired cases, with a larger difference before the Omicron (incidence rate ratio: 4.49, 95% confidence interval: 2.02, 9.99) than during the Omicron period (incidence rate ratio: 1.62, 95% confidence interval: 1.44, 1.82). Intensive care unit admission was associated with 30-day mortality for hospital-acquired (adjusted odds ratio: 4.4, 95% confidence interval: 2.3-8.4) and non‐hospital-acquired cases (adjusted odds ratio: 4.0, 95% confidence interval: 3.5-4.7). Conclusions Hospital-acquired COVID-19 infections remain significant, associated with higher mortality rates than non-hospital-acquired infection and disproportionately affecting older patients. Implications for public health Our findings underscore the need for robust hospital COVID-19 infection prevention strategies.

title: Differences in health status among workers who acquired COVID-19 at work compared to workers who sustained a non-COVID-19 work-related injury or illness, 18-months post-injury/infection.
abstract: Objective: To compare the physical and mental health status of workers who experienced work-related COVID-19 infections versus workers with other types of work-related injuries, 18 months after the initial work absence. Methods: We collected survey data from 1,000 workers with workers’ compensation claims between July and October 2022, and examined differences in seven self-reported physical and mental health outcomes. Potential outcome mediation models examined factors associated with observed differences in health outcomes. Results: We observed better self-rated health, physical role function, and less psychological distress among respondents with COVID-19 compared to non-COVID-19 claims. Reporting a disagreement with the workers’ compensation agency partially explained these differences. Conclusions: Despite concern over the long-term health impacts of COVID-19 infections, workers with COVID-19 infections reported similar or better health than those with non-COVID-19 work-related injuries, 18 months later.

title: Wait times at Christchurch Hospital for adjuvant breast irradiation and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: This study aimed to quantify wait times for adjuvant breast radiotherapy at Christchurch Hospital following surgery or completion of chemotherapy, with specific attention to the impact of COVID-19 lockdowns on service delivery. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of patients with breast cancer who initiated adjuvant radiotherapy between 1 January 2018 and 31 December 2022 at Christchurch Hospital. Wait times were defined as the interval (in days) from final surgery or chemotherapy to the first fraction of radiotherapy. Median wait times were tabulated and graphed to determine trend lines accounting for the COVID-19 lockdown periods affecting Canterbury, New Zealand. RESULTS: The cohort included 682 patients. Median wait time to radiotherapy from surgery was 72 days and from adjuvant chemotherapy was 36 days. A statistically significant increase in wait times was observed from surgery to radiotherapy of 7.2 days per annum (95% confidence interval 6.84-7.65 days, p<0.001). An initial increase in wait times was followed by a comparative reduction during the COVID-19 lockdown period. CONCLUSION: Wait times for adjuvant breast radiotherapy have increased at Christchurch Hospital from 2018 to 2022. Although COVID-19 restrictions temporarily reduced delays, sustained increases suggest multifactorial pressures. Excessive delays to commencing radiation should be minimised to reduce the risk of locoregional recurrence.

title: Association of the COVID-19 lockdown and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) in Korean adolescents
abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is a worldwide pandemic that causes anxiety. Research on possible risk factors for anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic is scarce. In this study, we examined 54,890 participants' web-based self-reported data from the Korea Youth Risk Behavior Web-based Survey in 2020. The Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 questionnaire was used to measure anxiety levels. The prevalence of anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 score ≥ 10) was 11.2%. Anxiety in adolescents during the COVID-19 pandemic was significantly associated with female gender (odds ratio [OR] = 1.29, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.02-1.09), low family affluence scale (OR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.03-1.34), economic aid (OR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.01-1.23), financial difficulties caused by COVID-19 (OR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.11-1.26), substance use (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.05-1.37), asthma (OR = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.08-1.37), allergic rhinitis (OR = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01-1.15), atopic dermatitis (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.01-1.17), severe stress (OR = 10.01, 95% CI: 8.40-12.03), perceived unhealthy status (OR = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.52-1.82), perceived unhappiness (OR = 2.30, 95% CI: 2.12-3.11), internet addiction (OR = 1.97, 95% CI: 1.85-2.10), school violence experience (OR = 1.59, 95% CI: 1.29-1.97), depression (OR = 2.78, 95% CI: 2.60-2.97), suicidal ideation (OR = 1.94, 95% CI: 1.79-2.11), suicidal plan (OR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.30-1.69), and suicidal attempt (OR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.04-1.45). These results highlight the risk factors for anxiety and offer a straightforward method for identifying teenagers who are more likely to experience anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Vaccine imprinting drives increased SARS-CoV-2 variant infection in children
abstract: Virus exposure history, particularly first exposure, is believed to shape vaccine efficacy and infection susceptibility; however, evidence for mechanistic links between immune responses in individuals and epidemiological outcome in populations is scarce. Recent co-circulation of SARS-CoV-2 variants XFG and BA.3.2 has revealed a striking enrichment in BA.3.2 cases among children. By combining epidemiological modeling, serology and monoclonal antibody analysis in children and adults, we show the dependence of effective variant-specific antibodies on vaccination history which may explain birth-year influence on differential susceptibility to these co-circulating variants. Ancestral cross-reactive site I antibodies frequently neutralize BA.3.2, but not XFG. By contrast, Omicron type-specific site I/III and III antibodies frequently neutralize XFG but not BA.3.2, revealing a tradeoff in the ability to neutralize these two co-circulating strains. These findings mechanistically link immune history, variant neutralization, antibody repertoire and variant infection risk, and suggest that vaccination regimens in children should prioritize neutralization breadth.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Virus exposure history, especially first exposure, is believed to shape vaccine efficacy and infection susceptibility, yet mechanistic links between immune responses and epidemiological outcomes are scarce. Recent co‐circulation of SARS‐CoV‐2 variants XFG and BA.3.2 has revealed a striking enrichment of BA.3.2 cases among children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study performed an observational analysis of children and adults, integrating epidemiological modeling with serological testing to assess variant‐specific antibody responses. The focus was on vaccination history and antibody titers in these participants.
analysis.methods: The study combined epidemiological modeling with serology and monoclonal antibody analysis in children and adults to evaluate the dependence of variant‐specific antibody levels on vaccination history. Antibody neutralization assays quantified the ability of sera to block XFG and BA.3.2 infection.
analysis.main_results: Children exhibited a marked enrichment of BA.3.2 infections compared with other variants, indicating increased susceptibility. Ancestral cross‐reactive site I antibodies neutralized BA.3.2 but not XFG, whereas Omicron‐type‐specific site I/III and III antibodies neutralized XFG but not BA.3.2, revealing a tradeoff in antibody specificity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors explain that prior vaccination history shapes the antibody repertoire, accounting for the birth‐year–related differential susceptibility of children to BA.3.2. They propose that pediatric vaccination strategies should prioritize broad neutralization, providing a mechanistic link between immune history and variant risk.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings indicate that children’s vaccination regimens should aim to elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies, guiding vaccine design and public‐health measures to mitigate BA.3.2 risk. Understanding the relationship between immune history and variant susceptibility also informs surveillance and therapeutic monitoring.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to an abstract with no detailed sample size, control groups, or confounder assessment, making the findings preliminary and of moderate confidence. Further studies with larger, well‐controlled cohorts are needed to confirm the mechanistic links between immune history and variant susceptibility.

analysis.summary_en: The preprint investigates why children appear more susceptible to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variant BA.3.2 than to XFG, despite both circulating simultaneously. By reviewing epidemiological data and performing serological and monoclonal antibody analyses in children and adults, the authors show that BA.3.2 cases are enriched in pediatric populations. They find that ancestral cross‐reactive site I antibodies neutralize BA.3.2 but not XFG, whereas Omicron‐type‐specific site I/III and III antibodies neutralize XFG but not BA.3.2, indicating a trade‐off in antibody specificity. The study links this pattern to vaccination history, suggesting that prior immunization shapes the antibody repertoire and drives differential susceptibility. Consequently, the authors argue that pediatric vaccination programs should focus on inducing broad, cross‐variant neutralizing antibodies to reduce infection risk. These results provide a mechanistic explanation for the birth‐year effect on variant susceptibility and highlight the importance of antibody breadth in future vaccine strategies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 病毒暴露史,尤其是首次暴露,被认为影响 疫苗 的疗效和感染易感性,但 疫苗 与流行病学结果之间的机制联系很少。最近 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 变种 XFG 和 BA.3.2 的共同传播揭示了儿童中 BA.3.2 病例的惊人丰富。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究对儿童和成人进行了观察分析,将流行病学模型与血清学测试相结合,以评估变异特异性抗体反应。重点是这些参与者的 疫苗接种 病史和抗体滴度。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究将流行病学模型与 血清学 以及儿童和成人的单克隆抗体分析相结合,以评估变异特异性抗体水平对 疫苗接种 历史的依赖性。抗体中和测定定量了血清阻断 XFG 和 BA.3.2 感染的能力。
elements_zh.main_results: 与其他变体相比,儿童表现出 BA.3.2 感染的显着富集,表明易感性增加。祖先交叉反应位点 I 抗体中和 BA.3.2 但不中和 XFG,而 Omicron 型特异性位点 I/III 和 III 抗体中和 XFG 但不中和 BA.3.2,这揭示了抗体特异性的权衡。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,先前的 疫苗接种 历史塑造了抗体库,解释了儿童对 BA.3.2 的出生年份相关的差异易感性。他们建议儿科 疫苗接种 策略应优先考虑广泛的中和,在免疫史和变异风险之间提供机制联系。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,儿童 疫苗接种 方案应旨在引发广泛中和抗体,指导 疫苗 设计和公共卫生措施,以减轻 BA.3.2 风险。了解免疫史和变异易感性之间的关系也可为 监测 和治疗监测提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据仅限于摘要,没有详细的样本量、对照组或混杂因素评估,因此研究结果是初步的且可信度中等。需要对更大规模、控制良好的 队列研究 进行进一步研究,以确认免疫史和变异易感性之间的机制联系。

source_body_en: Virus exposure history, particularly first exposure, is believed to shape vaccine efficacy and infection susceptibility; however, evidence for mechanistic links between immune responses in individuals and epidemiological outcome in populations is scarce. Recent co-circulation of SARS-CoV-2 variants XFG and BA.3.2 has revealed a striking enrichment in BA.3.2 cases among children. By combining epidemiological modeling, serology and monoclonal antibody analysis in children and adults, we show the dependence of effective variant-specific antibodies on vaccination history which may explain birth-year influence on differential susceptibility to these co-circulating variants. Ancestral cross-reactive site I antibodies frequently neutralize BA.3.2, but not XFG. By contrast, Omicron type-specific site I/III and III antibodies frequently neutralize XFG but not BA.3.2, revealing a tradeoff in the ability to neutralize these two co-circulating strains. These findings mechanistically link immune history, variant neutralization, antibody repertoire and variant infection risk, and suggest that vaccination regimens in children should prioritize neutralization breadth.

title: Provincializing vulnerability: Rethinking communication inequality in East Asia's COVID-19 research.
abstract: This article examines how East Asian COVID-19 scholarship conceptualizes vulnerable groups and communication inequality, and what this regional corpus contributes to comparative health communication and the sociology of epidemics. Drawing on bibliometric mapping and article-level thematic coding of 184 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 on China, Japan, and South Korea, the study compares East Asia-focused research with global COVID-19 literature. The findings show that East Asian scholarship tends to define vulnerability through situational system mismatch. Children, students, older adults, women, people with disabilities, chronic disease patients, and low-income groups become vulnerable when crisis governance disrupts the institutions, platforms, family relations, and support systems on which they depend. The article further identifies four mechanisms through which communication inequality intensifies vulnerability: institutional and technological exclusion, failures of understanding and judgment, interruptions of support, and governance exposure and stigma amplification. Even within East Asia, the literature shows important internal differences. Japanese studies foreground aging and norm pressure, Chinese studies emphasize urban-rural educational inequality and youth vulnerability, and Korean studies appear closer to global research in their attention to digital inequality, gendered isolation, discrimination, and health management. By bringing East Asian scholarship into comparative pandemic research, this article shows how vulnerability can be generated through everyday system configurations and crisis communication infrastructures. It argues that future pandemic preparedness requires inclusive communication systems alongside medical and epidemiological capacity.

title: Inequalities in mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection for people with severe mental illness during and following vaccination roll-out in England: a retrospective, whole-country linked cohort study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: People with severe mental illness (SMI) had a higher risk of death following SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with people without SMI during the COVID-19 pandemic peak. It is unclear whether this risk reduced in later stages after vaccination roll-out. We aimed to assess all-cause and cause-specific mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection in people with or without SMI across pandemic stages, using whole-country data, while accounting for sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. METHODS: In this retrospective, whole-country cohort study, we analysed linked electronic health records for all people in England registered to primary care who were alive in November, 2019 (>99% of the population). The study population included people who had COVID-19 between Jan 31, 2020, and June 30, 2023, with information on deaths and vaccination. Data extracted from the NHS England Secure Data Environment provided through the British Heart Foundation Data Science Centre CVD-COVID-UK-COVID-IMPACT Consortium linked datasets were curated to form a dataset in July, 2024. Cox regression estimated differences in all-cause and COVID-19 mortality. Analyses were stratified by pandemic stages, defined by WHO policy and UK Government vaccination roll-out: Jan 31-Sept 30, 2020 (stage 1); Oct 1, 2020-July 18, 2021 (stage 2, vaccination roll-out); and July 19, 2021-June 30, 2023 (stage 3, post-vaccination roll-out). SMI comprised schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, or other affective and non-affective disorder with psychosis. A patient and public involvement panel was consulted during design phases of the study. FINDINGS: 13 463 945 people with COVID-19 were identified, of whom 160 190 (1·19%) had SMI. People with SMI were older [mean age [SD], SMI 49·7 years [17·9], non-SMI 45·0 years [17·6]), had a similar sex split (females SMI vs non-SMI: 56·3% vs 56·6%); and were mostly White British (77·3% or 76·3%). People with SMI had higher all-cause mortality than those without (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1·56, 95% CI 1·53-1·59). All-cause mortality risk in people with SMI was elevated in stage 1 (aHR 1·27, 95% CI 1·22-1·32), but larger in the stage 2 (aHR 1·56, 1·51-1·61) and stage 3 (aHR 1·55, 1·50-1·59). Vaccination prevalence was initially higher for people with SMI (in stage 2: 112 795 [73·2%, 95% CI 72·9-73·4], compared with people without SMI, 8 852 970 [67·4%, 67·3-67·4]). By study end, fewer people with SMI were fully vaccinated (127 145 [79·4%, 79·2-79·6]), compared with people without SMI (11 605 915 [87·2%, 87·2-87·3]. Higher COVID-19 mortality risk in people with SMI persisted but was partially attenuated by vaccination (aHR 1·25, 1·17-1·34). INTERPRETATION: Excess mortality in people with SMI persisted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Preventive public health and clinical strategies are needed to address excess mortality and lower vaccination. FUNDING: Health Foundation-Academy of Medical Sciences.

title_original: Inequalities in mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection for people with severe mental illness during and following vaccination roll-out in England: a retrospective, whole-country linked cohort study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: People with severe mental illness (SMI) experienced higher mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection during pandemic peaks, but it was unclear whether this risk persisted after vaccination roll-out. The study addressed a knowledge gap by examining whether excess mortality in people with SMI changed across pandemic stages defined by vaccination roll-out.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective, whole-country cohort study used linked electronic health records from England covering over 99% of the population registered to primary care. The study population included 13,463,945 people with COVID-19 between January 31, 2020, and June 30, 2023, with data on deaths and vaccination status.
analysis.methods: Cox regression models estimated differences in all-cause and COVID-19 mortality between people with and without SMI, stratified by pandemic stages defined by WHO policy and UK vaccination roll-out. SMI was defined as schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, or other affective and non-affective disorders with psychosis.
analysis.main_results: People with SMI had higher all-cause mortality than those without (adjusted hazard ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.53–1.59). The elevated risk was present in stage 1 (aHR 1.27, 1.22–1.32) and increased in stages 2 (aHR 1.56, 1.51–1.61) and 3 (aHR 1.55, 1.50–1.59). By study end, fewer people with SMI were fully vaccinated (79.4%) compared with those without SMI (87.2%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as showing that excess mortality in people with SMI persisted throughout the pandemic despite vaccination, though vaccination partially attenuated COVID-19 mortality risk (aHR 1.25, 1.17–1.34). The novelty lies in quantifying persistent disparities across pandemic stages using whole-country linked data.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for targeted public health and clinical strategies to reduce excess mortality and improve vaccination uptake among people with SMI, particularly given their elevated risk across all pandemic stages.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s reliance on routine health records may introduce misclassification or residual confounding, and generalisability to settings without universal healthcare is uncertain. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and potential unmeasured confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective, whole-country cohort study in England assessed mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection among 13,463,945 people with COVID-19, including 160,190 with severe mental illness (SMI). Using linked electronic health records and Cox regression, the authors found that people with SMI had persistently higher all-cause mortality than those without SMI across all pandemic stages, with adjusted hazard ratios of 1.27 in stage 1, 1.56 in stage 2, and 1.55 in stage 3. Vaccination partially attenuated COVID-19 mortality risk (aHR 1.25), but by study end, fewer people with SMI were fully vaccinated (79.4%) compared with those without SMI (87.2%). The authors conclude that excess mortality in people with SMI persisted despite vaccination, underscoring the need for targeted public health and clinical strategies to address disparities and improve vaccination coverage.

analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s reliance on routine health records may introduce misclassification or residual confounding, and generalisability to settings without universal healthcare is uncertain. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and potential unmeasured confounding.

title_zh: 英格兰在和后续疫苗接种推广期间,严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2感染后患有严重精神疾病人群的死亡率不平等:一项回顾性全国范围关联队列研究研究
source_body_en: BACKGROUND: People with severe mental illness (SMI) had a higher risk of death following SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with people without SMI during the COVID-19 pandemic peak. It is unclear whether this risk reduced in later stages after vaccination roll-out. We aimed to assess all-cause and cause-specific mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection in people with or without SMI across pandemic stages, using whole-country data, while accounting for sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. METHODS: In this retrospective, whole-country cohort study, we analysed linked electronic health records for all people in England registered to primary care who were alive in November, 2019 (>99% of the population). The study population included people who had COVID-19 between Jan 31, 2020, and June 30, 2023, with information on deaths and vaccination. Data extracted from the NHS England Secure Data Environment provided through the British Heart Foundation Data Science Centre CVD-COVID-UK-COVID-IMPACT Consortium linked datasets were curated to form a dataset in July, 2024. Cox regression estimated differences in all-cause and COVID-19 mortality. Analyses were stratified by pandemic stages, defined by WHO policy and UK Government vaccination roll-out: Jan 31-Sept 30, 2020 (stage 1); Oct 1, 2020-July 18, 2021 (stage 2, vaccination roll-out); and July 19, 2021-June 30, 2023 (stage 3, post-vaccination roll-out). SMI comprised schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, or other affective and non-affective disorder with psychosis. A patient and public involvement panel was consulted during design phases of the study. FINDINGS: 13 463 945 people with COVID-19 were identified, of whom 160 190 (1·19%) had SMI. People with SMI were older [mean age [SD], SMI 49·7 years [17·9], non-SMI 45·0 years [17·6]), had a similar sex split (females SMI vs non-SMI: 56·3% vs 56·6%); and were mostly White British (77·3% or 76·3%). People with SMI had higher all-cause mortality than those without (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1·56, 95% CI 1·53-1·59). All-cause mortality risk in people with SMI was elevated in stage 1 (aHR 1·27, 95% CI 1·22-1·32), but larger in the stage 2 (aHR 1·56, 1·51-1·61) and stage 3 (aHR 1·55, 1·50-1·59). Vaccination prevalence was initially higher for people with SMI (in stage 2: 112 795 [73·2%, 95% CI 72·9-73·4], compared with people without SMI, 8 852 970 [67·4%, 67·3-67·4]). By study end, fewer people with SMI were fully vaccinated (127 145 [79·4%, 79·2-79·6]), compared with people without SMI (11 605 915 [87·2%, 87·2-87·3]. Higher COVID-19 mortality risk in people with SMI persisted but was partially attenuated by vaccination (aHR 1·25, 1·17-1·34). INTERPRETATION: Excess mortality in people with SMI persisted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Preventive public health and clinical strategies are needed to address excess mortality and lower vaccination. FUNDING: Health Foundation-Academy of Medical Sciences.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 在大流行高峰期间感染 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 后,患有严重精神疾病 (SMI) 的人经历了更高的 死亡率,但尚不清楚在 疫苗接种 推出后这种风险是否持续存在。该研究通过检查 SMI 患者中过多的 死亡率 是否在 疫苗接种 推出定义的大流行阶段发生变化,解决了知识差距。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调,需要采取有针对性的公共卫生和临床策略,以减少 SMI 患者过多的 死亡率 并提高 疫苗接种 的吸收率,特别是考虑到他们在所有大流行阶段的风险都较高。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究对常规健康记录的依赖可能会导致错误分类或残留混杂,并且在没有全民医疗保健的情况下的普遍性尚不确定。由于观察设计和潜在的未测量混杂因素,证据强度中等。

title: Impact of COVID-19 Pandemic Restrictions on Maxillofacial and Oral Surgery Services at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital.
abstract: BACKGROUND The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in a limitation of health care services to mainly emergency cases and widespread curtailment of routine clinical services. OBJECTIVE To evaluate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions on maxillofacial and oral surgery (MFOS) services. METHODS We conducted a retrospective, record review study of MFOS patients managed between 26 March and 28 December 2020 (COVID-19 period) and compared these with the same pre-COVID period 1 year previously. Data collected included variables such as patient diagnoses, type of treatment, and treatment setting. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the distribution of diagnoses and treatment procedures, and trends were illustrated using line graphs. Comparisons between the 2 periods were performed using χ2 tests, with a P-value of <0.05 considered statistically significant. RESULTS A total of 2926 patients were consulted during the COVID-19 period, constituting a 41.88% decline (5032 in 2019 versus 2926 in 2020) (P<0.0001). General anesthetic procedures decreased from 453 cases in 2019 to 272 in 2020, a 39.96% reduction (P=0.000448). Trauma-related diagnoses decreased from 249 cases in 2019 to 154 cases in 2020 (P=0.556). The largest drop was observed in alert levels 4 and 5. Trauma was the most frequent diagnosis in the COVID-19 period, followed by sepsis and pathology. The 19- to 35-year age group recorded the highest number of cases across all periods. CONCLUSION The COVID-19 pandemic and the implementation of the national lockdown resulted in a substantial decline in MFOS services. Our findings suggest that regulating alcohol sales and distribution can have a positive impact on reducing trauma admissions.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review evaluates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions on maxillofacial and oral surgery (MFOS) services at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital. The central question is how these restrictions affected the volume and types of surgical procedures and diagnoses during the pandemic period compared to the pre-pandemic period.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a retrospective, record review study comparing MFOS patients managed during the COVID-19 period (26 March to 28 December 2020) with the same pre-COVID period one year earlier. analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The study found a substantial decline in MFOS services during the pandemic, with a 41.88% reduction in patient consultations (from 5032 in 2019 to 2926 in 2020, P<0.0001). General anesthetic procedures also decreased by 39.96% (from 453 to 272 cases, P=0.000448). Trauma-related diagnoses decreased from 249 to 154 cases (P=0.556), but trauma remained the most frequent diagnosis during the pandemic. The largest drop in services was observed in alert levels 4 and 5.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not provide detailed information on the specific mechanisms or reasons behind the decline in trauma-related diagnoses, nor does it explore the broader implications of these changes on patient outcomes or healthcare systems. The study focuses on descriptive statistics and does not address potential confounding factors or long-term effects.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings suggest that pandemic restrictions significantly impacted MFOS services, particularly in high alert levels. The review implies that regulating alcohol sales and distribution could help reduce trauma admissions, highlighting the need for targeted public health interventions to mitigate the indirect effects of the pandemic on surgical services.

abstract_zh: 背景 新型冠状病毒感染 大流行导致医疗保健服务仅限于主要针对紧急病例,并广泛削减常规临床服务。目的 评估 新型冠状病毒感染 大流行限制对颌面和口腔外科 (MFOS) 服务的影响。方法 我们对 2020 年 3 月 26 日至 12 月 28 日(新型冠状病毒感染 期间)管理的 MFOS 患者进行了回顾性记录审查研究,并将这些患者与 1 年前的新冠肺炎爆发前的相同时期进行了比较。收集的数据包括患者诊断、治疗 类型和 治疗 设置等变量。使用描述性统计总结诊断和 治疗 程序的分布,并使用折线图说明趋势。2个时期之间的比较采用χ2检验,P值<0.05被认为有统计学意义。结果 新型冠状病毒感染 期间共咨询了 2926 名患者,下降了 41.88%(2019 年为 5032 例,2020 年为 2926 例)(P<0.0001)。全身麻醉手术从2019年的453例减少到2020年的272例,减少了39.96%(P=0.000448)。创伤相关诊断从 2019 年的 249 例减少到 2020 年的 154 例(P=0.556)。在警报级别 4 和 5 中观察到最大的下降。创伤是 诊断 期间最常见的 诊断,其次是脓毒症和病理。19 岁至 35 岁年龄组的病例数在所有时期都是最高的。结论 新型冠状病毒感染 大流行和国家封锁的实施导致 MFOS 服务大幅下降。我们的研究结果表明,规范酒精销售和分销可以对减少创伤入院产生积极影响。

analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 研究发现,疫情期间MFOS服务大幅下降,患者咨询量减少了41.88%(从2019年的5032人次减少到2020年的2926人次,P<0.0001)。全身麻醉手术也减少了 39.96%(从 453 例减少到 272 例,P=0.000448)。与创伤相关的诊断从 249 例减少到 154 例(P=0.556),但创伤仍然是大流行期间最常见的 诊断。服务下降幅度最大的是警报级别 4 和 5。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述没有提供有关创伤相关诊断下降背后的具体机制或原因的详细信息,也没有探讨这些变化对患者结果或医疗保健系统的更广泛影响。该研究侧重于描述性统计,并未解决潜在的混杂因素或长期影响。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 调查结果表明,大流行限制严重影响了 MFOS 服务,特别是在高度戒备状态下。该审查表明,规范酒精销售和分销可能有助于减少创伤入院率,强调需要采取有针对性的公共卫生干预措施,以减轻大流行对外科服务的间接影响。
